episodes.title: Den store befolkningsudskiftning, Jensen Huangs comeback og årets julesang
episodes.description:
I ugens Radio Information tager vi den helt store tur rundt i Socialdemokratiets fortsatte højredrejning. Vi går bag om Nvidia-chefens overraskende comeback, og så synger vi julen ind.
---

Befolkningsudskiftning. Dét ord har nærmest fyldt alt i dansk politik, siden Mette Frederiksen i sidste uge i podcasten Borgerlig Tabloid trak begrebet fri af det ekstreme højre og plantede det lige midt i sit eget socialdemokratiske vokabularium. 

Statsministerens udtalelser debatteres nu heftigt både herhjemme og i udlandet, hvor højrenationale kræfter på den ene side hylder hende for at have modet til at tale om tingene, som de er – mens flere europæiske kolleger kalder hendes sprogbrug for »en katastrofe«. 

I dagens udgave af Radio Information tager vi den helt store tur rundt i temaet: Hvor kommer ideen om den store udskiftning fra, hvilke former for betydning bærer begrebet med sig, hvad siger debatten om tilstanden i dansk politik lige nu – og er der en grænse for Socialdemokratiets højredrejning? Anton Geist, Laura Friis Wang og Matthias Dressler-Bredsdorff udgør panelet.

Men der er også plads til andet. Rune Lykkeberg udlægger den vilde udvikling i sagen om Jen-Hsun ’Jensen’ Huang, der – med hjælp fra Donald Trump – nu er tilbage i spidsen for techvirksomheden Nvidia. 

Og endelig lægger Kristian Villesen vejen forbi for at fortælle om »Juletræet med sin pynt«, der både rummer julens storhed og ironiens befriende punktering – og som samtidig er den melodi, der i år skal rimes på i Informations traditionsrige julesangskonkurrence.

episodes.description: Is NVIDIA better off without Jensen Huang—or is losing its visionary founder the biggest risk to its future?After Jensen Huang's departure as CEO, NVIDIA faces a question that matters far beyond Silicon Valley: Can a world-leading technology company keep innovating without the person who built it? Should its next CEO be a technologist or a professional manager?In this episode of Experience Matters with Milton & John, two generations of entrepreneurs take opposite sides. Milton Chang, an 85-year-old Caltech-trained entrepreneur who took two companies public, believes NVIDIA may become stronger with a professional leadership team. John Barrera, a Silicon Valley entrepreneur, argues that replacing a visionary during the AI revolution could be an enormous mistake.🎼 **MILTON: A GREAT COMPANY NEEDS A CONDUCTOR, NOT A SUPERSTAR**Milton argues that NVIDIA has built extraordinary competitive advantages that won't vanish with one executive. At this scale, the CEO's job is to coordinate exceptional leaders across engineering, product, sales, and operations—not personally make every critical decision.His analogy: A great orchestra doesn't need its conductor to play every instrument. Could a strong management team actually unlock more innovation?🚀 **JOHN: YOU CAN'T REPLACE VISION WITH A COMMITTEE**John pushes back. NVIDIA is not a conventional mature business. AI is evolving fast, and the engineers building tomorrow's chips need a leader they believe in. Stock options alone may not keep the best people.He asks whether Jensen's relationships, technological instincts, and willingness to make big bets are harder to replace than a CEO title suggests.🍎 **APPLE, INTEL, AND THE PRICE OF LOSING A FOUNDER**We debate what happened after Steve Jobs left Apple, the strengths and limitations of Tim Cook's leadership, and lessons from Intel's history. Can a great operator still miss the next big shift?⚖️ **WHAT SHOULD NVIDIA'S BOARD DO NEXT?**With CFO Colette Kress serving as interim CEO, we debate two very different paths:• Milton would build a strong leadership team, develop a successor, and consider Jensen in a strategic advisory role.• John would favor bringing Jensen back if legally and practically possible—or ensuring NVIDIA is led by a visionary technologist.We agree on one important point: NVIDIA needs a better succession plan. We disagree on who should lead it.**THE BIG TAKEAWAY:** Is a legendary founder a company's greatest competitive advantage—or its greatest dependency? episodes.title: El ESCÁNDALO de NVIDIA que hizo caer a Jensen Huang
episodes.description:
¿Qué ha pasado con NVIDIA y por qué ha renunciado Jensen Huang? El escándalo que sacude al gigante de los chips de inteligencia artificial ha abierto una historia de relaciones personales, sospechas de espionaje, China y una batalla tecnológica de miles de millones de dólares.

El 12 de noviembre de 2026, NVIDIA anunció la salida de Jensen Huang, su histórico CEO y cofundador, después de 33 años al frente de la compañía. Pero, ¿qué hay realmente detrás de esta crisis? ¿Es un escándalo personal o estamos ante algo mucho más importante para el futuro de la inteligencia artificial?

La historia de los chips y la ley de Moore

Descubrimos cómo nacieron los semiconductores, por qué la ley de Moore impulsó décadas de innovación y cómo Estados Unidos llegó a depender de una red internacional de fabricación de microchips.

Taiwán, TSMC y la guerra tecnológica entre Estados Unidos y China

¿Por qué Taiwán es tan importante para la fabricación de chips? ¿Qué papel desempeña TSMC en el desarrollo de las GPU de NVIDIA? ¿Por qué Estados Unidos restringe la exportación de semiconductores avanzados a China?

El escándalo de Jensen Huang y las sospechas de espionaje

Analizamos las informaciones sobre las relaciones personales del antiguo CEO, la empresa Megaspeed de Singapur, los posibles desvíos de chips hacia China y las investigaciones que han rodeado la crisis.

¿Pudo existir una operación de espionaje? ¿Qué se sabe realmente y qué continúa siendo una hipótesis? ¿Está en peligro la burbuja de la inteligencia artificial?

NVIDIA se ha convertido en una de las empresas fundamentales de la revolución de la IA. Sus chips impulsan centros de datos, modelos de inteligencia artificial y una industria que mueve inversiones gigantescas.

Por eso, la salida de Jensen Huang plantea preguntas que van mucho más allá de una empresa: ¿puede una crisis de liderazgo afectar al futuro de la IA? ¿Quién controla realmente la tecnología más estratégica del mundo? ¿Qué papel tendrán China, Estados Unidos y Taiwán en los próximos años?

¿Crees que lo ocurrido en NVIDIA es principalmente un escándalo empresarial o podría tener consecuencias mucho mayores para la industria tecnológica?

episodes.title: Jensen Huang: The Media Missed the Real Story
episodes.podcast_title: The PR Breakdown with Molly McPherson
episodes.description:
On November 8, Jensen Huang sent an email to NVIDIA employees that started with six words: "I was unfaithful to my wife." The same day, NVIDIA's board said it had "no reason to believe" that national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, and the company said he would keep leading NVIDIA without interruption. Four days later he resigned. On the morning we recorded, he posted on X that if the board decides his return is in the best interest of the company, he would be honored to come back as CEO.

We go through how it got here. It starts with Megaspeed, the Singapore data center company U.S. officials suspected of helping NVIDIA chips reach China, and with New York Times reporting that officials believed a former Megaspeed executive close to Huang was working for Chinese intelligence. China calls that claim groundless, and the Justice Department says it has not reached a conclusion. Then came a second reported relationship, this one with an executive who reported directly to him, and his tenure ended in about a day.

I pulled the coverage through Muck Rack: about 280,000 articles in 10 days. The board's line "no reason to believe" ran in almost 19,000 of them, more than three times the coverage of Huang's own apology. I share what that tells us, why I read his post as a reapplication more than an apology, and what to listen for on Colette Kress's first earnings call as interim CEO. The lesson for any leader: don't reassure before you know.

Episode 119 — Jensen Huang: Overleveraged | Think Pieces and Conversations Podcast

How does one of the most powerful men in technology lose his position at the company he helped build? And what happens when personal decisions become vulnerabilities that money and influence cannot protect you from?

In Episode 119 of Think Pieces and Conversations, titled Jensen Huang: Overleveraged, I go beyond the headlines surrounding Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia, his extramarital affairs, and the allegations involving a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

We discuss power, politics, marriage, national security, and whether Huang's personal relationships left him exposed to pressures he couldn't control. If the allegations surrounding China were so serious, why haven't they resulted in treason charges? And how much leverage can someone gain over a billionaire with secrets to protect?

But there's another development that caught my attention.

The mysterious RTX 5090 shortage.

Before Huang resigned, Nvidia's flagship graphics card had become nearly impossible to find at normal retail prices. Rumors circulated that the RTX 5090 was being discontinued, with some listings approaching $10,000. Nvidia denied discontinuing the GPU.

Then, just days after Huang's departure, RTX 5090 inventory began reappearing at major retailers, including Newegg, with cards listed for thousands of dollars.

Why did these GPUs suddenly become available again?

I explore the timing, the theories surrounding Nvidia's relationship with China, and whether the events could be connected. There's no established evidence linking the inventory changes to Huang's resignation, but the timing raises questions worth examining.

Then we take the conversation into an entirely different territory: Are billionaires overleveraging themselves through marriage?

I compare Jensen Huang's personal choices with Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, examining divorce, family, financial exposure, and whether marriage becomes an unnecessary risk for men operating at that level of wealth and influence.

Is marriage a source of stability, or can it become one of the biggest vulnerabilities a powerful person creates?

This episode isn't simply about infidelity or graphics cards. It's about power, leverage, reputation, and the consequences of decisions made behind closed doors.

Because having billions of dollars doesn't necessarily mean you're the one holding all the leverage.

Jensen Huang walked out of the company he founded 33 years ago, and almost nobody outside tech could name who was left. In this episode of Where Pop Culture Meets PR, Jacki asks what happens when the founder is the brand and the founder falls. Why did one resignation wipe so much value off the share price? And what does a man like Huang do next?


The "Jensen premium" on the share price, the contrast with how Microsoft and Amazon spread the spotlight, and board decisions at Intel and McDonald's all show how one famous face can become a risk nobody planned for. Staff loyalty, strong as it was, runs straight into a board's duty to trust what it is told, and much of the reporting remains unconfirmed. The stakes reach past one boardroom to Huang's own next move and the choices open to his wife, Laurie Huang.


In this episode

  • The Jensen premium: Why analysts talk about a share-price premium for one person, and what a fall of as much as 14% in a day reveals.
  • One face, one jacket: How the keynotes, magazine covers and black leather jacket tied the company to the man inside it.
  • Sharing the spotlight: What Microsoft and Amazon did differently, and why Nvidia had no obvious successor the public knew.
  • Loyalty versus governance: Why a staff poll and thousands of supportive comments could not settle a question that belonged to the board.
  • Thank you, sorry, goodbye: The case for one short statement, a long quiet period and a second act built on action rather than words.
